relationship: Doeg's report about David and Abimelech
rationale: The heading names Doeg reporting to Saul that David came to Abimelech's house. Samuel records Doeg reporting Jesse's son's arrival with Abimelech at Nomba. The named report corresponds closely, while the heading calls Doeg Idumean and Samuel calls him Syrian; those ethnic descriptions are not harmonized.

relationship: Boasting by workers of lawlessness
rationale: The accusation of boasting in wickedness and lawlessness all day long corresponds to the question about sinners boasting and workers of lawlessness speaking injustice. Both challenge the wrongdoers' boastful speech rather than merely describing their power.

relationship: The tongue as a sharpened weapon
rationale: The source joins a tongue devising injustice with deceit worked like a sharpened razor; Psalm 63 describes tongues sharpened like a sword. The particular comparison joins harmful speech and cutting blades, with razor and sword remaining different weapons.

relationship: Loving evil rather than good
rationale: The preference for wickedness over goodness corresponds to John's account of people loving darkness more than light because their deeds are evil. The connection concerns the stated preference for evil, without identifying the psalm's addressee with a particular person in John's account.

relationship: Uprooted wickedness and enduring righteous roots
rationale: The petition that God remove the wrongdoer's root from the land of the living contrasts with the assurance that righteous roots will not be uprooted. The common root-and-uprooting image gives opposite outcomes for the wicked and righteous.

relationship: The righteous observe the wrongdoer's judgment
rationale: The righteous seeing, fearing and laughing at the wrongdoer's overthrow compares with the righteous rejoicing when he sees vengeance in Psalm 57. The responses differ, and the latter's washing hands in sinners' blood is not imported into this source.

relationship: Trust in abundant wealth instead of God
rationale: The person who failed to make God his helper and hoped in abundant wealth exemplifies the misplaced hope against which 1 Timothy warns the wealthy. The instruction expressly contrasts hope in uncertain wealth with hope in God.

relationship: A flourishing tree in God's house
rationale: The speaker's fruitful olive tree in God's house corresponds to the righteous trees planted in the Lord's house and flourishing in His courts. The olive remains distinct from the palm and cedar named in Psalm 91.

relationship: The Maeleth designation in headings
rationale: Both headings preserve the designation Maeleth. Psalm 87 adds answering and names Heman the Israelite; the shared designation is retained without assigning it an unprovided musical meaning or equating the two headings in full.

relationship: Parallel fool and corruption declaration
rationale: The fool's denial of God and the account of corrupt, abominable conduct correspond to the opening running text of Psalm 13. The complete target also contains its heading; this is a comparison of the actual declaration, not a renumbering of that composite unit.

relationship: Parallel divine inspection for understanding
rationale: The source says God bent down from heaven to see whether anyone understands or seeks God; Psalm 13 says the Lord looked down for that purpose. The inspection and its question correspond, while bent down and looked down, and God and Lord, remain the respective formulations.

relationship: Parallel universal departure and absence of good
rationale: Both declarations say all turned aside and became useless. The source then says no one is doing good, while the opening of the complete expanded Psalm 13:3 unit says none shows kindness. The target's additional throat, tongue, feet and fear clauses remain part of that unit and are not attributed to this source verse.

relationship: The doing-good declaration and Romans' kindness wording
rationale: Romans' scriptural citation includes all turning aside and becoming useless, then says no one shows kindness, corresponding to the psalm's no one doing good. Psalm 13 also contains the declaration, so this connection does not claim that Psalm 52 is the exclusive source of Romans' wording.

relationship: Parallel devouring of the people as bread
rationale: Both passages question workers of lawlessness who devour the people as a meal of bread and fail to call on God. The distinctive meal-of-bread image and the accompanying failure to invoke God establish the literary correspondence.

relationship: Parallel fear where there is no fear, with different explanations
rationale: The prospect of fear where there is no fear corresponds to Psalm 13's report of cowering there. This source explains the result through scattered bones of people-pleasers and God's rejection, while Psalm 13 says God is with a righteous generation; the explanations and tense are preserved distinctly.

relationship: Parallel salvation from Zion and restored captivity
rationale: The question about Israel's salvation from Zion and the rejoicing of Jacob and Israel when captivity is turned back correspond directly. The passage is retained as a literary parallel without assigning either declaration to a particular historical restoration.

relationship: The Ziphites' question to Saul about hidden David
rationale: The heading's question about David being hidden among the Ziphites closely corresponds to their question to Saul in 1 Samuel 23. The named speakers, addressee and report supply the connection; the later Ziphite report in chapter 26 does not establish a unique date for the heading.

relationship: Attackers who do not set God before themselves
rationale: Both passages describe attackers rising against the speaker, strong men seeking his soul, and their failure to set God before themselves. The source calls them outsiders while Psalm 85 calls them lawless people; the shared sequence is not an identification of an individual enemy.

relationship: Evil returning upon its perpetrators
rationale: The expectation that evils will be turned back upon enemies corresponds to the wrongdoer's trouble returning upon his own head. The comparison concerns the reversal of inflicted evil, with the source's further petition for destruction preserved separately.

relationship: Sacrifice joined to thanksgiving
rationale: The source promises willing sacrifice and thanksgiving to God's good name; Psalm 115 explicitly promises a sacrifice of praise. Both join sacrificial offering with praise, without turning the source's willing offering into a specified mandatory rite.

relationship: Rescue from every affliction
rationale: The psalm reports rescue from every affliction, while David's speech in Samuel asks for shelter and expresses the assurance that the Lord will rescue him from every affliction. The distinctive formula connects testimony with future assurance without dating the psalm to that encounter.

relationship: Fear accompanied by darkness
rationale: The speaker's fear, trembling and covering darkness compare with the great dark fear falling on Abram during his sunset trance. The source's covering darkness and Genesis' description of a dark fear remain distinct formulations in different circumstances.

relationship: Flying like a dove
rationale: The wish for a dove's wings to fly away and rest compares with Isaiah's question about those flying like doves with their young. The bird-flight image is shared, but Isaiah's arriving company is not identified with the psalmist's desired escape.

relationship: Retreat to a remote wilderness lodging
rationale: The speaker's distant flight and lodging in the wilderness correspond to Jeremiah's wish for a remote wilderness station where he could leave his faithless people. One reports retreat and the other desires it; no common physical lodging is asserted.

relationship: Rescue from inward distress and a storm
rationale: The speaker reports waiting for rescue from faintheartedness and tempest. Psalm 106 recounts mariners whose souls melted in distress before they cried to God and He quieted the storm. The combined distress-and-storm rescue provides the comparison without making this speaker one of those sailors.

relationship: Divided tongues in a troubled city
rationale: The appeal to divide their tongues amid the city's lawlessness corresponds to God's confounding languages and interrupting the city-building project in Genesis. The link concerns divine disruption of human speech; it does not identify the psalm's city as Babel.

relationship: Interest-taking within a corrupt city
rationale: The source places interest-taking and deceit in the city's squares; Ezekiel accuses his addressed city of taking interest and increase amid oppression. The particular economic wrong in an urban indictment supplies the connection.

relationship: A trusted companion and leader becomes unsafe
rationale: The address to a man of like soul, the speaker's leader and acquaintance, stands within the complaint about intimate betrayal. Micah warns against confidence in friends and hope in leaders. The shared intimate and leadership roles support the comparison without naming this companion.

relationship: Shared food and violated fellowship
rationale: The recollection of making food sweet together and walking in concord in God's house corresponds to the trusted man who ate the speaker's loaves and magnified treachery in Psalm 40. The source's food is preserved as food, rather than replaced with a familiar wording about sweet counsel.

relationship: Going down alive to Hades
rationale: The appeal that the wicked descend alive to Hades uses the distinctive fate narrated of Korah's company when the earth swallowed them. The parallel concerns that extraordinary living descent, not an identification of the psalm's enemies as the same people.

relationship: Three daily occasions of prayer
rationale: The source names evening, morning and noon for recounting and proclaiming before God. Daniel continues making supplication three times a day despite the royal restriction. The threefold daily practice corresponds, but Daniel's target verse does not name the psalm's three hours.

relationship: God existing before the ages
rationale: The description of God as existing before the ages corresponds to the prayer addressing Him as God before the mountains and from age to age. The connection is the explicit assertion of God's existence beyond created time, not an explanation of the source's separate no-exchange clause.

relationship: Profaning a covenant contrasted with God's pledge
rationale: The source says they profaned his covenant; Psalm 88 records God's pledge not to profane His covenant. The repeated covenant-profanation expression supports a contrast, without resolving the source's pronouns into the parties of Psalm 88's covenant.

relationship: Oily pleasantness and sharp harm
rationale: The source calls words softer than oil yet missiles. Proverbs moves from honey-dripping lips and the temporary oiling of the listener's throat to what proves bitter and sharper than a blade. Both juxtapose pleasant oral imagery with weapon-like harm, while preserving whose throat appears in Proverbs.

relationship: Casting one's care upon God
rationale: The instruction to cast one's care upon the Lord corresponds closely to 1 Peter's instruction to cast all anxiety upon Him because He cares. The source emphasizes nourishment and the righteous person's stability, while Peter explicitly gives God's care as the reason.

relationship: The shortened life of the wicked
rationale: The declaration that men of blood and deceit will not live half their days corresponds to Proverbs' contrast between the fear of the Lord adding days and impious years becoming few. Proverbs does not specify the source's fraction of half a lifetime.

relationship: Trampling and persistent fighting (same-chapter)
rationale: The source joins a man's trampling with his all-day fighting and afflicting the speaker. Verse 3 joins enemies' all-day trampling with many fighters from a height. This same-chapter recurrence varies the singular and plural attackers and the placement of the all-day modifier.

relationship: Trampling and persistent fighting (same-chapter)
rationale: The source's enemies trampled all day and are many fighters from a height; the preceding verse has one man trampling, fighting all day and afflicting the speaker. This same-chapter recurrence preserves the different subjects and the placement of the all-day modifier.

relationship: Fear and hope answered by confidence (same-chapter)
rationale: This verse says that by day the speaker will fear but will hope in God; verse 12 joins hope in God with the declaration that he will not fear. The same-chapter contrast preserves the positive fear statement here rather than silently negating it.

relationship: Fearlessness and the question of human harm
rationale: The source's hope in God, refusal to fear and question about what flesh can do correspond to Hebrews' cited confidence in the Lord as helper, refusal to fear and question about what a person will do. The comparison concerns that closing confidence, while the source's opening phrase remains my words.

relationship: Watching for the heel
rationale: The concealed enemies watching the speaker's heel compare with God's statement that the serpent will watch for the woman's seed's heel. The uncommon heel-watching expression supplies the link; it does not identify these human enemies as the serpent.

relationship: Tears set before and seen by God
rationale: The source says God set the speaker's tears before Himself; God's message to Hezekiah says He has seen his tears. Both explicitly place a distressed person's tears before divine notice, without introducing a bottle or equating the two sufferers.

relationship: Enemies turned backward by God
rationale: The expectation that enemies will turn backward on the day the speaker calls on God corresponds to Psalm 17's report that God made enemies turn their backs. Future expectation and reported victory remain distinct; no common battle is asserted.

relationship: Trust without fear of a human being
rationale: The source's hope in God, refusal to fear and question about what a human can do correspond closely to the confidence cited in Hebrews. The connection is the shared fear-and-human-harm formula, without claiming this psalm is Hebrews' exclusive quotation source.

relationship: Paying vows made to God
rationale: The speaker's vows of praise and promise to pay them correspond to Deuteronomy's requirement not to delay payment of a vow to the Lord. The law also distinguishes not making a vow from making one and then failing to fulfill it.

relationship: Soul rescued from death and feet from slipping
rationale: Both passages combine rescue of the soul from death and feet from slipping with being well pleasing before God. The source names the light of the living, while Psalm 114 names the land of the living and additionally mentions eyes rescued from tears.

relationship: Hope beneath God's wings
rationale: The source seeks shelter in the shadow of God's wings until lawlessness passes; Psalm 90 assures the addressee that he will hope under God's wings. The shared wing-shelter image is specific, while the source's stated duration remains its own.

relationship: Divine qualities sent to guide and rescue
rationale: The source reports God sending His mercy and truth; Psalm 42 asks God to send His light and truth and recounts their guidance to His holy mountain and dwellings. Both portray divine qualities as sent aid, with mercy and light remaining distinct.

relationship: The human tongue as a sharp sword
rationale: The source compares human tongues to a sharp sword alongside weapon-like teeth. Psalm 63 likewise describes tongues sharpened like a sword. The connection rests on this exact speech-weapon image, not on changing Psalm 63's bitter deed into a bitter word.

relationship: Parallel exaltation above heaven and earth
rationale: The appeal for God to be exalted above the heavens and for His glory over all the earth corresponds directly to the refrain in Psalm 107. The parallel is the complete heaven-and-earth exaltation formula.

relationship: The trap-maker falls into his own pit
rationale: The source reports enemies preparing a trap and digging a pit into which they fell. Psalm 7 describes the wrongdoer digging a pit and predicts his fall into the hole he made. Their reversal of the intended victim and trap-maker supplies the connection.

relationship: Parallel ready heart and resolve to sing
rationale: The repeated declaration that the heart is ready and the resolve to sing and make music correspond to Psalm 107's opening song declaration. The latter joins the music to my glory, which is not silently added to this source's wording.

relationship: Parallel awakening of instruments and dawn
rationale: The summons to awaken, the psaltery and lyre, and the speaker's awakening at dawn correspond closely to Psalm 107. The source's address to his glory is preserved distinctly from the target's distribution of glory in its preceding verse.

relationship: Parallel praise among peoples and nations
rationale: Both passages promise thanksgiving among peoples and music among nations. The matched two-part public praise formula belongs to the larger shared song sequence rather than merely a general command to worship.

relationship: Mercy and truth reaching heaven and clouds
rationale: Both passages associate God's great mercy with heaven and His truth with the clouds. The source's extent to the heavens and Psalm 107's above the heavens remain distinct formulations within the same paired image.

relationship: Closing reprise of the exaltation refrain (same-chapter)
rationale: The closing appeal for exaltation above the heavens and glory over all the earth repeats verse 6. This same-chapter refrain frames the intervening account of the enemies' pit and the speaker's readiness to sing.

relationship: The Do not destroy heading designation
rationale: Both headings explicitly contain Do not destroy. The source names David and the target Asaph; the shared designation is retained without identifying a musical tune, common occasion or author beyond what each heading says.

relationship: A question challenging human justice
rationale: The question about speaking righteousness and judging uprightly among the sons of men corresponds to Micah's question whether Israel's authorities should know justice. The questioning form challenges their moral responsibility, while the groups addressed remain distinct.

relationship: Weaving injustice and weaving lawless works
rationale: The source says hands weave injustice; Isaiah describes weaving a spider's web and explains that the works are works of lawlessness. The textile-making image gives concrete form to deliberate wrongdoing in both passages.

relationship: Wrongdoing described from the womb
rationale: The source describes sinners as estranged from the womb and going astray from the belly with lies. Isaiah addresses a faithless people called lawless even from the belly. The shared birth-origin language is preserved as accusation in each context, not generalized into a new claim about every infant.

relationship: Serpent and asp imagery for harmful wickedness
rationale: The source likens their fury to a serpent and describes a deaf asp; Deuteronomy calls their wine the venom of serpents and asps. The paired serpent-and-asp imagery corresponds, but fury is not rewritten as venom and the target's wine remains its own image.

relationship: Snakes beyond the charmer's control
rationale: The asp's refusal to hear enchanters corresponds to Jeremiah's deadly snakes that cannot be charmed. The distinctive failure of snake-charming provides the connection without identifying the metaphorical wicked people with Jeremiah's sent snakes.

relationship: God crushes the teeth of the wicked
rationale: The broken teeth and crushed grinders of lions correspond to Psalm 3's declaration that God crushed sinners' teeth. The source's lion imagery intensifies the same tooth-breaking representation of disabling hostile power.

relationship: Wickedness melting like wax before fire
rationale: The source's melting wax and falling fire compare with Psalm 67's wish that sinners perish as wax melts before fire. The common wax-and-fire destruction image does not erase the source's further statement about not seeing the sun.

relationship: Blood imagery in the aftermath of vengeance
rationale: The righteous person's washing hands in sinners' blood compares with Psalm 67's foot dipped in blood and dogs' tongues associated with enemies. Both portray the aftermath of divine vengeance through bodily contact with enemy blood, while hands, foot and dogs remain distinct.

relationship: A visible distinction between righteous and wicked
rationale: The concluding affirmation of fruit for the righteous and God judging them on earth compares with Malachi's challenge about the advantage of serving God and the promised visible distinction between righteous and lawless people. The psalm's verdict and Malachi's future vindication address the particular question of whether righteousness has a discernible result.

relationship: Saul's watchers at David's house
rationale: The heading's account of Saul sending and watching the house to kill David corresponds to Samuel's account, which explicitly supplies messengers at David's house, Michal's warning and her escape assistance. The named sender, house watch and intended killing establish the narrative link.

relationship: Separation from lawless people and men of blood
rationale: The plea for rescue from workers of lawlessness and men of blood corresponds to the plea not to be destroyed with the ungodly and men of blood whose hands hold lawless deeds. Rescue from these people and avoidance of their fate remain different petitions.

relationship: Innocence and pursuit of the soul
rationale: The source protests that the pursuit of his soul is not for his lawlessness or sin. Psalm 7 places injustice in the speaker's hands and repayment to those who repay him evils within a conditional oath leading to enemy pursuit of his soul. Both relate pursuit to the speaker's conduct; Psalm 7:5 does not expressly supply the object of his repayment.

relationship: Awakening God to meet the afflicted
rationale: The appeal that God awake, meet the speaker and see compares with Psalm 43's calls to awake, arise, help and redeem during affliction. The specific awakening appeal is shared without identifying the individual and communal situations as one event.

relationship: God's judgment extending to all nations
rationale: The invocation of the God of Israel to attend to all nations corresponds to the call for God to rise and judge the earth, taking inheritance among all nations. The particular movement from Israel's God to the whole range of nations connects the petitions.

relationship: Human opponents pictured as hungry dogs
rationale: The source compares the evening city-circlers to hungry dogs; Isaiah describes shameless dogs who know no satisfaction. The canine appetite image is shared, while the source's hunger does not by itself assert Isaiah's explicit insatiability.

relationship: A sword in hostile speech
rationale: The sword on their lips corresponds to the sharp sword of the human tongue in Psalm 56. Both place a cutting weapon in an organ of speech, preserving lips here and tongue in the target.

relationship: God laughs at hostile nations
rationale: The Lord's laughter and treatment of nations as nothing correspond to the heavenly One laughing and sneering at the hostile coalition in Psalm 2. The laughter of God at collective opposition is the particular shared response.

relationship: Supporter confession with a changed address (same-chapter)
rationale: The address to my strength and resolve to keep watch toward God return in verse 18 as an address to my helper and resolve to make music. The repeated confession of God as supporter links this same-chapter modified refrain without making the different addresses identical.

relationship: Sinful lips and entrapment
rationale: The source joins sins of the mouth and lips with a petition that they be caught in their arrogance. Proverbs states that a sinner falls into traps through the sin of lips. The shared mouth-sin and entrapment pattern compares a petition for judgment with a stated consequence of wrongdoing.

relationship: Judgment leading to recognition of worldwide divine rule
rationale: The source predicts that they will know God rules Jacob and the ends of the earth. Psalm 82 petitions for humiliating judgment and recognition that the Lord alone is Most High over all the earth. Both connect judgment with acknowledgment of God's worldwide rule, preserving prediction here and petition there.

relationship: Return of the evening dog refrain (same-chapter)
rationale: The return at evening, hunger like dogs and circling the city repeat verse 7. This same-chapter recurrence follows the petitions for judgment and precedes the further description of their search for food.

relationship: Morning proclamation of divine mercy
rationale: The speaker resolves to sing to God's power and exult in His mercy in the morning; Psalm 91 calls for declaring His mercy in the morning. The specified morning celebration of mercy supplies the connection, while Psalm 91 additionally assigns truth to the night.

relationship: Closing supporter confession with music (same-chapter)
rationale: The closing address to my helper and promise to make music reprise verse 10's confession of God as supporter. This same-chapter variation changes the earlier address my strength and watchfulness into helper and song, while adding the addresses my God and my mercy.

relationship: The heading concerning those who will be changed
rationale: The source's heading concerning those who will yet be changed corresponds to Psalm 44's heading concerning those who will be changed. The shared supplied designation is preserved without replacing it with a different musical or floral title.

relationship: Anger and renewed divine compassion
rationale: The source places God's anger beside His compassion after rejection and overthrow. Isaiah's thanksgiving explicitly remembers God's anger turning away and His mercy. The connection is this movement between anger and compassion; Isaiah states the turning away more expressly.

relationship: Healing a fracture after divine affliction
rationale: The appeal to heal the earth's fractures after God shook it compares with Isaiah's announcement that the Lord will heal His people's fracture and wounded pain. The healing-of-fracture expression is shared, while earth and people remain different immediate objects.

relationship: Judgment pictured as an intoxicating drink
rationale: The source says God gave the people wine of stupor. Isaiah describes Jerusalem drinking the Lord's cup of anger and falling, then expressly calls her drunk but not from wine. The judgment-as-intoxication imagery corresponds without changing that qualification.

relationship: Parallel rescue of the beloved by God's right hand
rationale: Both passages ask for salvation by God's right hand and a hearing so that His beloved ones may be rescued. The ordered beloved-rescue, right-hand and hearing clauses provide a close literary parallel.

relationship: Parallel divine allotment of Shechem and the valley of tents
rationale: Both report God speaking in His holy place before the division of Shechem and measurement of the valley of tents. Within that divine speech the source says I will exult and the target I will be exalted; those different clauses remain distinct within the shared allotment sequence.

relationship: Parallel claims over Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim and Judah
rationale: The same ordered territorial declarations culminate in Ephraim's relation to the divine speaker's head and Judah as My king. The source edition's king wording is preserved instead of replacing it with a familiar lawgiver wording.

relationship: Parallel Moab, Idumea and subjected foreign peoples
rationale: Both combine Moab as a vessel of My hope, the sandal extended over Idumea and foreign peoples subjected. The source calls Moab a basin and Psalm 107 a cauldron; neither is rewritten as a washbasin.

relationship: Parallel questions about the enclosed city and Idumea
rationale: The paired questions about who will lead to an enclosed city and who will guide as far as Idumea correspond directly. Neither passage names that city, so the connection does not supply an identification such as Petra.

relationship: Parallel declaration that God will not go out with the forces
rationale: Both passages ask about the God who rejected them and then state that He will not go out with their forces. The negative is preserved; the connection is not rewritten as a promise that God will accompany the army.

relationship: Parallel help in affliction and futile human salvation
rationale: Both ask for help from affliction because human salvation is futile. The matched petition and its reason connect the two passages as part of the repeated song section.

relationship: Parallel power in God and the enemies' reduction to nothing
rationale: The resolve to act mightily in God and His bringing hostile people to nothing correspond to Psalm 107's closing resolve and assurance. The source's afflicting people and the target's enemies remain the respective descriptions.

relationship: God raises the distressed speaker upon a rock
rationale: The account of crying from the ends of the earth with a weary heart and being raised upon a rock corresponds to Psalm 26's protection in trouble and raising upon a rock. The distinctive upward placement on the rock supplies the link without adding a higher-than-I phrase.

relationship: Enduring residence in God's dwelling
rationale: The resolve to sojourn in God's dwelling for ages compares with dwelling in the Lord's house for length of days in Psalm 22. Both anticipate enduring divine hospitality, while the source also names shelter under God's wings.

relationship: Inheritance associated with fear of God
rationale: The source associates God's gift of inheritance with those fearing His name. Psalm 24 describes the person who fears the Lord and declares that his seed will inherit land. The target specifies descendants and land beyond what this source specifies.

relationship: God adds length of life to the king
rationale: The future addition of days to the king's days and years through generations corresponds to Psalm 20's king asking for life and receiving length of days. The source's future assurance and the target's reported gift are preserved distinctly.

relationship: Royal permanence before God
rationale: The king remaining before God for ever corresponds to David's prayer that the house of God's servant remain before God for ever. The common royal permanence formula does not equate the individual king with the entire house or explain away the source's following question about mercy and truth.

relationship: Praise joined to payment of vows
rationale: The promise of enduring music to God's name and daily fulfillment of vows corresponds to Psalm 49's paired commands to offer praise and pay vows to the Most High. The shared praise-and-vow combination connects promise with instruction.

relationship: Jeduthun named in both headings
rationale: Both headings explicitly name Jeduthun with a David attribution. This is a comparison of the exact supplied heading name, without extending it to differently spelled names elsewhere or assigning an unprovided office.

relationship: Question and command for the soul's submission (same-chapter)
rationale: The question about the soul submitting to God is resumed in verse 6 as a command to the soul. This same-chapter variation gives salvation as the reason here and endurance in verse 6, rather than making the two reasons identical.

relationship: Savior and supporter refrain with a changed result (same-chapter)
rationale: The confession that God is savior and supporter recurs in verse 7. The result here is not being shaken any further, while verse 7 says not migrating away; this same-chapter variation preserves that actual difference.

relationship: A vulnerable wall and collapse imagery
rationale: The assault on a human is compared to a leaning wall and a fence thrust down. Isaiah likens sin to a wall falling in a captured fortified city and then to shattered pottery. The unstable-wall image corresponds, while its human and moral referents remain distinct.

relationship: Peaceful or blessing mouths with evil hearts
rationale: The source contrasts blessing with the mouth and cursing with the heart. Psalm 27 describes people speaking peace to neighbors while evils are in their hearts. The particular outward-speech and inward-intention opposition supplies the connection.

relationship: Command resuming the soul's submission question (same-chapter)
rationale: The command that the soul submit to God resumes verse 2's question. This same-chapter response grounds submission in endurance from God, whereas the earlier verse names salvation.

relationship: Repeated supporter confession preserving migration wording (same-chapter)
rationale: The savior-and-supporter confession repeats verse 3, but its concluding assurance is that the speaker will not migrate away. The earlier assurance that he will not be shaken is a related yet differently worded same-chapter result and does not replace this clause.

relationship: Pouring the inner self before God
rationale: The instruction to pour out hearts before God corresponds to Hannah's explanation that she is pouring out her soul before the Lord while praying. The shared pouring-out image connects exhortation with enacted prayer, preserving hearts here and soul there.

relationship: Falsehood, scales and injustice
rationale: The source says the sons of men are false upon scales for doing injustice; Proverbs calls deceitful scales an abomination and a just weight acceptable. The comparison follows the supplied falsehood-and-scales language, without substituting conduct for the sons of men or claiming they weigh less than breath.

relationship: Refusing to attach the heart to increasing wealth
rationale: The warning not to attach the heart when wealth flows corresponds to the instruction that the rich not set hope on uncertain wealth but on God. The source also condemns injustice and plunder, but it does not therefore label every increase of wealth as plunder.

relationship: Repayment to each according to works
rationale: The declaration that God will repay each according to his works corresponds directly to Romans' statement within its account of impartial divine judgment. The formula is shared without asserting an exclusive quotation source for Romans.

relationship: The soul thirsting for God
rationale: The source's thirsty soul and longing flesh in a waterless land correspond to Psalm 41's deer-water comparison and thirst of the soul for the living God. The particular metaphor directs physical thirst toward desire for God in both passages.

relationship: Blessing God with lifted hands
rationale: The promise to bless God during life and lift hands in His name corresponds to Psalm 133's instruction to lift hands toward the holy places and bless the Lord. The gestures and blessing correspond, while the target explicitly situates its instruction by night.

relationship: Divine abundance pictured as rich nourishment
rationale: The wish that the soul be filled as with fat and richness compares with Psalm 35's promised intoxication from the richness of God's house and drink from His delight. The abundant nourishment imagery connects a wish with an assurance without making both passages descriptions of the same literal meal.

relationship: Remembrance on the bed and dawn meditation
rationale: The source conditionally speaks of remembrance on the bed and meditation on God at dawn. Psalm 118 describes eyes awake before dawn to meditate on His sayings. The connection preserves the condition, the different timing and the distinction between God and His sayings as meditation's object.

relationship: Exultation in the shelter of God's wings
rationale: The speaker promises to exult beneath God's wings because God became his helper. Psalm 16 appeals for protection and declares that God will shelter the speaker beneath His wings. The shared wing-shelter image connects promised exultation with protective petition and assurance.

relationship: God's right hand supports the speaker
rationale: The declaration that God's right hand supported the speaker corresponds directly to the same assurance in Psalm 17. The source's soul clinging behind God and the target's further discipline clauses remain their respective surrounding descriptions.

relationship: Hostile people descending to the earth's depth
rationale: The enemies who sought the speaker's soul will enter the lowest earth. Ezekiel describes nations bringing Egypt's daughters down dead into the earth's depth with those descending to a pit. The descent image connects distinct judgment scenes without identifying their victims.

relationship: The slain become portions for animals
rationale: The source joins delivery to the sword with becoming portions for foxes. Jeremiah says the people's dead will become food for birds and wild beasts. The aftermath of death as animal food corresponds, while the animals and judged groups remain different.

relationship: Righteous joy and the stopped mouth of injustice
rationale: The source links the king's future rejoicing in God with the past statement that the mouth speaking unjust things was stopped. Psalm 106 predicts the upright seeing and rejoicing and all lawlessness stopping its mouth. The paired joy and silencing pattern corresponds while the past and future stopping remain distinct.
